title: The logistics of buying/owning a barbell
summary: With gyms closed, NH explains what to consider before buying a home barbell: without plates and a rack it is mostly for floor pulls, so buy quality from a reputable brand, try the bar beforehand, and maintain it with oil, brushing and proper storage.
claims: A barbell alone does not make a gym: without a rack or stands you are mostly limited to pulls from the floor
Do not clean a barbell onto your back to squat without a rack; the risk-to-reward ratio is skewed toward risk
Barbells are available now only because plates and racks are not; a bar without plates is useless and without a rack loses much of its utility
If possible, wait and buy a whole gym bundle at once with the barbell, which is more efficient and saves money
Buy the highest-quality bar you can from a reputable company; a good bar lasts 10-20 years, so spending around $400 is worth it
Cheap $100 bars from unknown sites feel terrible and bend permanently with around 400 lb, while a good bar flexes and returns to straight
Buy a bar you have already trained with for weeks; he used his bar for two years before buying his own
Many high-quality bars are stiff, so if you dislike stiff bars, test before buying
Bars with cosmetic flaws, like those from Rogue's boneyard, can save money; his saved about $100 and he cannot tell the difference
Start a home gym with an Olympic barbell because it is the most versatile; do not buy 15 specialty bars you never use
The centerpiece of a home gym is the barbell and the rack
Non-chromed steel bars rust even in low humidity; oil and brush them often, since preventing rust is easier than removing it
Brush the bar after every chalk session; chalk clogs the knurling and kills grip, and the deep cleaning needed later can damage the bar
Store the bar horizontally on a wall or vertically in a holder like a sword to keep it off a cold, humid floor and away from your feet
